videos.script: Horta tried new insulated bags for a year: a hundred thousand deliveries with the old bags, a hundred thousand with the new. Deliveries in the new bags were faster, and the test says the difference is not chance. The p-value is about one in a hundred billion. {{year}} The difference is a third of a minute. Twenty seconds. {{twenty}} Both statements are true. The first says the difference is real. The second says how big it is, and that is the one a decision needs. {{both}} The word significant causes the trouble. In everyday speech it means important. In statistics it means only distinguishable from zero, and with enough data, everything that is not exactly zero becomes distinguishable. {{word}} The opposite mistake is just as common. A small study that finds nothing significant has often not found nothing. It has found too little to tell. {{opposite}} This last lesson gives the tools to tell them apart: effect sizes, a threshold for what matters decided in advance, and the confidence interval, which answers both questions at once. It ends with a checklist for every analysis in this course. {{checklist}}
